summary: Horizon is a web tool that answers one question quickly: can a lander at the Moon’s south pole get power and a direct link to Earth, and on which days? We computed real terrain horizons from NASA LOLA elevation data and combined them with NASA SPICE positions of the Sun and Earth, hour by hour for 2027. The app offers a site-by-day comparison grid and a horizon panorama showing the Sun and Earth at true angular size, above or hidden behind the ridge. Planners get annual sunlight, Earth-link and combined availability, the longest night and longest communications blackout, with uncertainty ranges; a plain-language mode serves educators and the public. We validated against NASA’s average-visibility maps: Sun availability matches within about one percentage point at Malapert and Nobile, and we openly report that Shackleton rim does not, because an 80 m terrain grid cannot resolve its knife-edge. Faster, transparent comparison of sites and dates helps teams plan safer, better-powered Artemis and commercial lunar landings.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Horizon answers one question for any Moon south pole landing site: on which days and hours does a lander have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication? It compares sites and dates across 2027 on a lit 3D Moon globe and a year grid. Opening a site shows a panorama of the real terrain horizon with the Sun and Earth drawn at true angular size, hour by hour, either above the ridge or hidden behind it. A stats panel reports annual sunlight, Earth link and combined availability, the longest night and the longest communications outage, with uncertainty ranges.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline reads NASA LRO LOLA south polar elevation data (80 m per pixel) and casts rays out to 150 km to compute the terrain horizon around each site. It combines this with NASA/NAIF SPICE positions of the Sun and Earth for every hour of 2027, corrected for the site's position on the surface. Visibility is the fraction of each disc above the horizon. The results are saved as static JSON files, so the website is fast and cheap to host.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Existing tools can give these answers, but their interfaces make quick comparison hard. Horizon lets mission planners screen sites and dates in seconds, lets educators show why the south pole is difficult, and lets the public see it with a plain-language mode. We aim to speed up early planning for Artemis and commercial lunar missions.

VALIDATION AND HONESTY

We compared our Sun availability with NASA's average-visibility maps. Malapert (-0.76 points) and Nobile (+1.00 points) agree closely, and the permanently shadowed Shackleton floor correctly shows no sunlight. Shackleton rim does not match, because an 80 m grid cannot resolve the narrow shadowed notch NASA's 60 m map shows there. We report this openly and show the range across neighbouring pixels and antenna heights (0, 2 and 10 m) instead of a single falsely precise number. The tool shows line-of-sight windows only, not a guarantee of power or a radio link.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, SpiceyPy) for processing; React, TypeScript and Vite for the web app; HTML canvas for the panorama; three.js for the globe; GSAP for transitions; hosted on Vercel. Data: NASA LOLA, SPICE kernels, NASA Blue Marble and the NASA SVS Moon map (Earth and Moon surface images are illustrations only).

CREATIVITY

The Sun and Earth are drawn at their real angular sizes, the ridge cuts them off when they set, Earth shows its true phase, and the globe is lit by the real Sun direction for the selected hour. The same results are shown for beginners and planners through a quick-answer mode and a detailed mode.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Three audiences, data resolution, antenna height, knife-edge sites, how "visible" is defined (any part of the disc), the single year of results, and clear limits stated in the app.

AI USE

We also used AI coding assistants (OpenCode and Claude) for planning, code generation and debugging. We chose the challenge and approach, ran the pipeline on NASA LOLA and SPICE data, and validated the results against NASA's average-visibility maps. All numbers in the app come from that pipeline.
